items.section_title: 1.9 · Objectives 1–7 — Heart failure: beta blockers
items.html: Beta blockers in heart failure. They can worsen heart failure, because lowering heart rate and contractility can decompensate a failing heart, so they were once avoided and classically considered contraindicated.
cites: Diuretics and Heart Failure Drugs.pptx, Slide 57

src.question: Why were beta blockers classically considered contraindicated in heart failure?
src.explanation: Correct. Lowering heart rate and contractility can decompensate a failing heart, so they were once avoided.

items.section_title: 1.7 · Objectives 1–2 — Heart failure: causes, types and compensation
items.html: Vasoconstriction in heart failure. Vasoconstriction is the compensatory response that increases afterload, because it raises the resistance the ventricle pumps against.
cites: Diuretics and Heart Failure Drugs.pptx, Slide 48

src.question: Which compensatory response in heart failure increases afterload?
src.explanation: Correct. Vasoconstriction raises the resistance the ventricle pumps against, or afterload.

items.section_title: 1.5 · Objectives 1–7 — Aldosterone and aldosterone antagonists
items.html: Aldosterone inside a collecting-duct cell. After binding its receptor and reaching the nucleus, aldosterone drives protein synthesis that adds sodium channels, increasing the number of sodium channels.
cites: Diuretics and Heart Failure Drugs.pptx, Slide 34

src.question: What does aldosterone do inside a collecting-duct cell?
src.key: Increases the number of sodium channels
src.explanation: Correct. After binding its receptor and reaching the nucleus, aldosterone drives protein synthesis that adds sodium channels.

items.section_title: 1.4 · Objectives 1–8 — Potassium-sparing diuretics
items.html: Amiloride acts in the collecting duct. Potassium-sparing diuretics act in the collecting duct, where about 2 to 3 percent of the sodium is reabsorbed under aldosterone control.
cites: Diuretics and Heart Failure Drugs.pptx, Slide 11

src.question: Amiloride acts at which site?
src.explanation: Correct. Potassium-sparing diuretics act in the collecting duct, where about 2 to 3 percent of the sodium is reabsorbed under aldosterone control.

items.section_title: 1.1 · Objectives 1–3 — Diuretics: the frame and the nephron
items.html: Furosemide acts in the thick ascending limb. Loop diuretics work in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, where about 25 percent of the sodium is reabsorbed.
cites: Diuretics and Heart Failure Drugs.pptx, Slide 12

src.question: Furosemide acts at which site?
src.explanation: Correct. Loop diuretics work in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, where about 25 percent of the sodium is reabsorbed.

items.section_title: 1.2 · Objectives 1–8 — Loop diuretics
items.html: Loop diuretics can be added to saline in hypercalcemia. Loop diuretics increase calcium excretion, so they can be added alongside saline in hypercalcemia, but saline hydration is the main treatment.
cites: Diuretics and Heart Failure Drugs.pptx, Slide 17

src.question: Which condition can a loop diuretic help treat when it is added to saline hydration, by increasing calcium excretion?
src.explanation: Correct. Saline hydration is the main treatment, and a loop diuretic can be added alongside it because loop diuretics increase calcium excretion.

also.explanation: Correct. Saline hydration is the main treatment, and loop diuretics can be added alongside it because they increase calcium excretion.

items.section_title: 1.2 · Objectives 1–8 — Loop diuretics
items.html: Gentamicin and loop diuretics. Aminoglycosides such as gentamicin have their ototoxicity potentiated by loop diuretics.
cites: Diuretics and Heart Failure Drugs.pptx, Slide 19

src.question: Which drug has its ototoxicity potentiated by loop diuretics?
src.explanation: Correct. Aminoglycosides such as gentamicin have their ototoxicity potentiated by loop diuretics.

items.section_title: 1.2 · Objectives 1–8 — Loop diuretics
items.html: Ototoxicity from loop diuretics. Ototoxicity, damage to the cochlea (classically described as hair-cell damage, though often reversible), is a listed adverse effect of loop diuretics such as furosemide.
cites: Diuretics and Heart Failure Drugs.pptx, Slide 18

src.question: Which drug can cause ototoxicity by damaging the cochlea, the hearing organ of the inner ear?
src.explanation: Correct. Ototoxicity, damage to the cochlea (classically described as hair-cell damage, though often reversible), is a listed adverse effect of loop diuretics such as furosemide.

items.section_title: 1.2 · Objectives 1–8 — Loop diuretics
items.html: Gout flare with loop diuretics. Loop diuretics decrease uric acid excretion and shrink plasma volume, so plasma levels rise, which concentrates uric acid and can precipitate gout.
cites: Diuretics and Heart Failure Drugs.pptx, Slide 15

src.question: A 64-year-old man with a history of gout starts a loop diuretic for ascites and develops a painful, swollen great toe ten days later. Which effect of the diuretic most likely triggered the flare?
src.key: Less uric acid excreted, so plasma levels rise
src.explanation: Correct. Loop diuretics decrease uric acid excretion and shrink plasma volume, which concentrates uric acid and can precipitate gout.

items.section_title: 1.2 · Objectives 1–8 — Loop diuretics
items.html: Calcium excretion: loops versus thiazides. Loop diuretics increase calcium (and magnesium) excretion, whereas thiazides decrease renal calcium excretion.
cites: Diuretics and Heart Failure Drugs.pptx, Slide 13

src.question: Which electrolyte excretion do loop diuretics increase but thiazide diuretics decrease?
src.explanation: Correct. Loop diuretics increase calcium (and magnesium) excretion, whereas thiazides decrease renal calcium excretion.

items.section_title: 1.2 · Objectives 1–8 — Loop diuretics
items.html: Hypokalemia from loop diuretics. Loop diuretics increase potassium excretion, and the resulting hypokalemia, low serum potassium, can cause weakness and cardiac arrhythmias.
cites: Diuretics and Heart Failure Drugs.pptx, Slide 18

src.question: A 59-year-old man with cirrhosis and ascites starts furosemide. Four days later he reports muscle weakness and palpitations. Which laboratory abnormality best explains his symptoms?
src.explanation: Correct. Loop diuretics increase potassium excretion, and the resulting hypokalemia can cause weakness and cardiac arrhythmias.

items.section_title: 1.3 · Objectives 1–8 — Thiazide diuretics
items.html: Volume depletion from thiazides. Excess salt and water loss leaves the patient volume depleted, which triggers reflex responses and orthostatic symptoms such as dizziness on standing, a falling blood pressure and dry mouth.
cites: Diuretics and Heart Failure Drugs.pptx, Slide 26

src.question: A patient on a thiazide is dizzy on standing with a falling blood pressure and dry mouth. Which adverse effect is most likely?
src.explanation: Correct. Excess salt and water loss leaves the patient volume depleted, which triggers reflex responses and orthostatic symptoms.

items.section_title: 1.3 · Objectives 1–8 — Thiazide diuretics
items.html: Hypokalemia from thiazides. Thiazides increase potassium excretion, and hypokalemia, a listed adverse effect, predisposes to cardiac arrhythmias.
cites: Diuretics and Heart Failure Drugs.pptx, Slide 26

src.question: Which electrolyte disturbance from thiazides contributes to cardiac arrhythmia risk?
src.explanation: Correct. Thiazides increase potassium excretion, and hypokalemia, a listed adverse effect, predisposes to cardiac arrhythmias.

items.section_title: 1.3 · Objectives 1–8 — Thiazide diuretics
items.html: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs weaken thiazides. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs block prostaglandins, which aid natriuresis, so this attenuates the natriuretic action of thiazides.
cites: Diuretics and Heart Failure Drugs.pptx, Slide 29

src.question: Why do nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs weaken the effect of thiazides?
src.key: They block the prostaglandins that aid natriuresis
src.explanation: Correct. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs block prostaglandins, which attenuates the natriuretic action of thiazides.

items.section_title: 1.4 · Objectives 1–8 — Potassium-sparing diuretics
items.html: Triamterene and potassium supplements. Avoid a supplement unless told otherwise, because triamterene already holds on to potassium, so a supplement can push potassium dangerously high and needs caution.
cites: Diuretics and Heart Failure Drugs.pptx, Slide 33

src.question: A patient taking triamterene asks about starting a potassium supplement. What is the best advice?
src.explanation: Correct. Triamterene already holds on to potassium, so a supplement can push potassium dangerously high and needs caution.

items.section_title: 1.4 · Objectives 1–8 — Potassium-sparing diuretics
items.html: Hyperkalemia from potassium-sparing diuretics. High serum potassium is the main adverse effect of potassium-sparing diuretics such as amiloride, and it is worse with angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors and potassium supplements.
cites: Diuretics and Heart Failure Drugs.pptx, Slide 33

src.question: A 67-year-old man with heart failure takes lisinopril and a potassium supplement. His physician adds amiloride. Two weeks later he has weakness and a slow, irregular pulse. Which laboratory abnormality is most likely?
src.explanation: Correct. Hyperkalemia is the main adverse effect of potassium-sparing diuretics, and it is worse with angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors and potassium supplements.

items.section_title: 1.5 · Objectives 1–7 — Aldosterone and aldosterone antagonists
items.html: Spironolactone with lisinopril. Lisinopril is an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor; both drugs raise serum potassium, so together the risk of hyperkalemia is high and potassium must be monitored.
cites: Diuretics and Heart Failure Drugs.pptx, Slide 33

src.question: Which combination carries the greatest risk of hyperkalemia?
src.explanation: Correct. Lisinopril is an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor; both drugs raise serum potassium, so together the risk of hyperkalemia is high and potassium must be monitored.

items.section_title: 1.5 · Objectives 1–7 — Aldosterone and aldosterone antagonists
items.html: Cirrhosis and aldosterone antagonists. Cirrhosis of the liver causes secondary hyperaldosteronism, which raises aldosterone, and aldosterone antagonists are used for the resulting edema.
cites: Diuretics and Heart Failure Drugs.pptx, Slide 37

src.question: Which condition raises aldosterone secondarily and is treated with an aldosterone antagonist?
src.explanation: Correct. Cirrhosis causes secondary hyperaldosteronism, and aldosterone antagonists are used for the resulting edema.

items.section_title: 1.6 · Objectives 1–7 — Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors
items.html: Laboratory monitoring with acetazolamide. Metabolic acidosis lowers bicarbonate, and potassium depletion lowers potassium, so watch for low bicarbonate and low potassium.
cites: Diuretics and Heart Failure Drugs.pptx, Slide 43

src.question: Which laboratory abnormalities should be watched in a patient taking acetazolamide?
src.explanation: Correct. Metabolic acidosis lowers bicarbonate, and potassium depletion lowers potassium.

items.section_title: 1.8 · Objectives 1–7 — Heart failure: diuretics and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors
items.html: Serum potassium: loops versus angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors. Loops increase potassium excretion, so they lower serum potassium, while angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors elevate it.
cites: Diuretics and Heart Failure Drugs.pptx, Slide 56

src.question: How do loop diuretics and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors differ in their effect on serum potassium?
src.key: Loops lower it and the inhibitors raise it
src.explanation: Correct. Loops increase potassium excretion, while angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors elevate serum potassium.

items.section_title: 1.12 · Objectives 1–7 — Aldosterone antagonists in heart failure and the other inotropic agents
items.html: Aldosterone antagonists slow heart failure progression. Neurohormonal inhibition of aldosterone slows remodeling of the left ventricle, and so slows heart failure progression.
cites: Diuretics and Heart Failure Drugs.pptx, Slide 73

src.question: Why do aldosterone antagonists slow progression of heart failure?
src.explanation: Correct. Neurohormonal inhibition of aldosterone slows remodeling of the left ventricle and so slows heart failure progression.

items.section_title: 1.12 · Objectives 1–7 — Aldosterone antagonists in heart failure and the other inotropic agents
items.html: Spironolactone eligibility in heart failure. Spironolactone holds on to potassium, so a potassium above 5 milliequivalents per liter excludes it, as does a high serum creatinine.
cites: Diuretics and Heart Failure Drugs.pptx, Slide 73

src.question: Which laboratory finding makes a heart failure patient ineligible for spironolactone?
src.explanation: Correct. Spironolactone holds on to potassium, so a potassium above 5 milliequivalents per liter excludes it, as does a high serum creatinine.

items.section_title: 1.12 · Objectives 1–7 — Aldosterone antagonists in heart failure and the other inotropic agents
items.html: Monitoring an aldosterone antagonist. Hyperkalemia is the main adverse effect, so serum potassium is the value to follow.
cites: Diuretics and Heart Failure Drugs.pptx, Slide 38

src.question: Which laboratory value is most important to monitor in a patient taking an aldosterone antagonist?
src.explanation: Correct. Hyperkalemia is the main adverse effect, so potassium is the value to follow.

items.section_title: 1.12 · Objectives 1–7 — Aldosterone antagonists in heart failure and the other inotropic agents
items.html: Milrinone and inamrinone inhibit phosphodiesterase 3. They inhibit cyclic adenosine monophosphate phosphodiesterase 3, which prevents breakdown of cyclic adenosine monophosphate, so it rises in the heart, giving direct stimulation of contraction.
cites: Diuretics and Heart Failure Drugs.pptx, Slide 74

src.question: Which enzyme do milrinone and inamrinone inhibit?
src.explanation: Correct. They inhibit cyclic adenosine monophosphate phosphodiesterase 3, raising cyclic adenosine monophosphate in the heart and giving direct stimulation of contraction.

also.explanation: Correct. Blocking phosphodiesterase 3 prevents breakdown of cyclic adenosine monophosphate, which stimulates contraction.

items.section_title: 1.12 · Objectives 1–7 — Aldosterone antagonists in heart failure and the other inotropic agents
items.html: Milrinone is an inotrope. Milrinone is a cyclic adenosine monophosphate phosphodiesterase (III) inhibitor, approved for short-term intravenous use in acute decompensated heart failure.
cites: Diuretics and Heart Failure Drugs.pptx, Slide 74

src.question: Which drug is an inotrope that works by inhibiting phosphodiesterase III and approved for short-term intravenous use?
src.explanation: Correct. Milrinone is a cyclic adenosine monophosphate phosphodiesterase (III) inhibitor, approved for short-term intravenous use in acute decompensated heart failure.

items.section_title: 1.12 · Objectives 1–7 — Aldosterone antagonists in heart failure and the other inotropic agents
items.html: Thrombocytopenia with phosphodiesterase III inhibitors. Thrombocytopenia is listed for these inotropes, with milrinone causing less than inamrinone, so inamrinone is more likely to cause it.
cites: Diuretics and Heart Failure Drugs.pptx, Slide 76

src.question: Which phosphodiesterase III inhibitor is more likely to cause thrombocytopenia?
src.explanation: Correct. Thrombocytopenia is listed for these inotropes, with milrinone causing less than inamrinone.

items.section_title: 1.10 · Objectives 1–3 — Digoxin: action, benefit and place
items.html: Adding digoxin in heart failure. Digoxin improves symptoms, exercise tolerance and quality of life and cuts hospitalizations, but it has no survival benefit, so expect fewer symptoms but no survival gain.
cites: Diuretics and Heart Failure Drugs.pptx, Slide 66

src.question: A 63-year-old man with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction remains symptomatic on optimal doses of an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor, a beta blocker and a diuretic. Which outcome should he expect from adding digoxin?
src.key: Fewer symptoms, but no survival gain
src.explanation: Correct. Digoxin improves symptoms, exercise tolerance and quality of life and cuts hospitalizations, but it has no survival benefit.

items.section_title: 1.11 · Objectives 5–8 — Digoxin toxicity, contraindications and the antidote
items.html: Digoxin contraindications: conduction and rate. Digoxin slows nodal conduction and the nodes further, so advanced atrioventricular block, severe bradycardia, sick sinus syndrome and Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome are listed contraindications.
cites: Diuretics and Heart Failure Drugs.pptx, Slide 71

src.question: Which conduction disorder contraindicates digoxin?
src.explanation: Correct. Digoxin slows nodal conduction, so advanced atrioventricular block is a contraindication.

also.explanation: Correct. Advanced atrioventricular block, severe bradycardia and Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome are listed contraindications to digoxin.
Correct. Advanced atrioventricular block and severe bradycardia are listed contraindications to digoxin, which slows nodal conduction.
Correct. Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome is listed among the contraindications to digoxin.

also.key: Severe bradycardia or sick sinus syndrome
also.explanation: Correct. Digoxin slows the nodes further, so severe bradycardia and sick sinus syndrome are contraindications.

items.section_title: 1.11 · Objectives 5–8 — Digoxin toxicity, contraindications and the antidote
items.html: Digoxin contraindications: ventricular rhythm. Premature ventricular beats and ventricular tachycardia are contraindications, because digoxin makes the ventricles more irritable.
cites: Diuretics and Heart Failure Drugs.pptx, Slide 71

src.question: Which ventricular rhythm problem contraindicates digoxin?
src.explanation: Correct. Premature ventricular beats and ventricular tachycardia are contraindications, because digoxin makes the ventricles more irritable.

items.section_title: 1.11 · Objectives 5–8 — Digoxin toxicity, contraindications and the antidote
items.html: Digoxin immune Fab. Its affinity for digoxin exceeds that of the sodium-potassium pump, so it binds digoxin more tightly, pulls it away and reverses toxicity rapidly.
cites: Diuretics and Heart Failure Drugs.pptx, Slide 72

src.question: How does digoxin immune Fab reverse toxicity?
src.key: It binds digoxin more tightly than the pump does
src.explanation: Correct. Its affinity for digoxin exceeds that of the sodium-potassium pump, so it pulls digoxin away and reverses toxicity rapidly.

items.section_title: 1.13 · Objectives 1–7 — Newer agents: ivabradine, sacubitril-valsartan, sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors
items.html: Ivabradine adverse effects. Ivabradine increases the risk of atrial fibrillation, causing new palpitations, and also of symptomatic bradycardia and visual phosphenes.
cites: Diuretics and Heart Failure Drugs.pptx, Slide 80

src.question: A 63-year-old man is starting ivabradine for heart failure. Which adverse effect should he be warned about?
src.explanation: Correct. Ivabradine increases the risk of atrial fibrillation, and also of symptomatic bradycardia and visual phosphenes.

items.section_title: 1.13 · Objectives 1–7 — Newer agents: ivabradine, sacubitril-valsartan, sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors
items.html: Ivabradine visual phosphenes. Visual phosphenes can resolve on their own, so the patient can be reassured and told to report persistent symptoms.
cites: Diuretics and Heart Failure Drugs.pptx, Slide 80

src.question: A patient on ivabradine notices brief brightness in part of the visual field. What should the patient be told?
src.key: It may resolve on its own
src.explanation: Correct. Visual phosphenes can resolve on their own, so the patient can be reassured and told to report persistent symptoms.

items.section_title: 1.13 · Objectives 1–7 — Newer agents: ivabradine, sacubitril-valsartan, sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors
items.html: Sacubitril-valsartan adverse effects. Hypotension, hyperkalemia, cough and renal insufficiency are the most common adverse effects, so watch for low blood pressure and high potassium.
cites: Diuretics and Heart Failure Drugs.pptx, Slide 81

src.question: A 70-year-old woman has just been switched from lisinopril to sacubitril-valsartan for heart failure. Which pair of adverse effects should be watched for most?
src.key: Low blood pressure and high potassium
src.explanation: Correct. Hypotension, hyperkalemia, cough and renal insufficiency are the most common adverse effects of sacubitril-valsartan.

items.section_title: 1.14 · Objectives 4 and 8–10 — Absorption, interactions, monitoring and patient education
items.html: Diuretic classes that deplete potassium. Loops, thiazides and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors; these three classes increase potassium excretion or deplete it.
cites: Diuretics and Heart Failure Drugs.pptx, Slide 43

src.question: Which diuretic classes deplete potassium?
src.key: Loops, thiazides and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors
src.explanation: Correct. These three classes increase potassium excretion or deplete it.

items.section_title: 1.2 · Objectives 1–8 — Loop diuretics
items.html: Volume depletion from loop diuretics. Too much sodium and water loss leaves the patient volume depleted, with orthostatic dizziness and dry mucous membranes.
cites: Diuretics and Heart Failure Drugs.pptx, Slide 18

src.question: A patient taking a loop diuretic is dizzy on standing and has dry mucous membranes. Which adverse effect is most likely?
src.explanation: Correct. Too much sodium and water loss leaves the patient volume depleted, with orthostatic dizziness and dry mucous membranes.

items.section_title: 1.3 · Objectives 1–8 — Thiazide diuretics
items.html: Thiazides and gout. Thiazides cause hyperuricemia, which can precipitate gout, so a history of gout argues against them.
cites: Diuretics and Heart Failure Drugs.pptx, Slide 26

src.question: Which preexisting condition makes a thiazide a poor choice because it can flare?
src.explanation: Correct. Thiazides cause hyperuricemia, which can precipitate gout, so a history of gout argues against them.

items.section_title: 2.4 · Objectives 1–7 — Class IB: lidocaine
items.html: Lidocaine and the atrioventricular node. Lidocaine's toxicity list includes increased atrioventricular conduction, along with hypersensitivity and its central nervous system effects.

src.question: Which cardiac effect is on lidocaine's toxicity list?
src.explanation: Lidocaine's toxicity list includes increased atrioventricular conduction, along with hypersensitivity and its central nervous system effects.

items.section_title: 2.6 · Objectives 1–8 — Class II: beta blockers
items.html: Class II and phase 4. Class II drugs decrease phase 4 depolarization, so pacemaker cells reach threshold later; they also slow conduction and prolong atrioventricular conduction.

src.question: Class II antiarrhythmics slow the heart mainly by which effect on pacemaker cells?
src.explanation: Class II drugs decrease phase 4 depolarization, so pacemaker cells reach threshold later; they also slow conduction and prolong atrioventricular conduction.

items.section_title: 2.8 · Objectives 1–7 — Class IV: verapamil, diltiazem
items.html: Class IV and a weak pump. Class IV drugs are negative inotropes, so verapamil and diltiazem are to be avoided in depressed cardiac function.

src.question: Why are class IV calcium channel blockers avoided in depressed cardiac function?
src.explanation: Class IV drugs are negative inotropes, so verapamil and diltiazem are to be avoided in depressed cardiac function.

items.section_title: 2.7 · Objectives 1–8 — Class III: amiodarone, dofetilide, sotalol
items.html: How class III prolongs repolarization. Class III drugs reduce potassium efflux, which prolongs phase 3 repolarization and the refractory period.

src.question: Class III antiarrhythmics prolong repolarization through which ion effect?
src.explanation: Class III drugs reduce potassium efflux, which prolongs phase 3 repolarization and the refractory period.

items.section_title: 2.7 · Objectives 1–8 — Class III: amiodarone, dofetilide, sotalol
items.html: Who can prescribe dofetilide. Dofetilide has limited availability, restricted to those with special training.

src.question: Which restriction applies to prescribing dofetilide?
src.explanation: Dofetilide has limited availability, restricted to those with special training.

items.section_title: 2.3 · Objectives 1–8 — Class IA: quinidine, procainamide, disopyramide
items.html: Quinidine's most frequent toxicity. Gastrointestinal upset (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea) is listed in 30 to 50 percent of patients.

src.question: Which adverse effect of quinidine occurs in 30 to 50 percent of patients?
src.explanation: Gastrointestinal upset (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea) is listed in 30 to 50 percent, quinidine's most frequent toxicity.

items.section_title: 2.3 · Objectives 1–8 — Class IA: quinidine, procainamide, disopyramide
items.html: Procainamide's short action. Procainamide has a short duration of action (3 to 4 hours), so a slow-release preparation is used.

src.question: Why is procainamide made as a slow-release preparation?
src.key: Its action lasts only 3 to 4 hours
src.explanation: Procainamide has a short duration of action (3 to 4 hours), so a slow-release preparation is used.

items.section_title: 2.9 · Objectives 1–8 — Miscellaneous agents: adenosine, digoxin, magnesium sulfate
items.html: Digoxin and autonomic tone. Digoxin indirectly increases parasympathetic tone and decreases sympathetic tone, slowing atrioventricular conduction.

src.question: What does digoxin do to autonomic tone on the heart?
src.explanation: Digoxin indirectly increases parasympathetic tone and decreases sympathetic tone, slowing atrioventricular conduction.

items.section_title: 2.9 · Objectives 1–8 — Miscellaneous agents: adenosine, digoxin, magnesium sulfate
items.html: Warning the patient before adenosine. Adenosine may stop the heart for 2 to 3 seconds, and flushing, shortness of breath and chest burning can follow.

src.question: What should a patient be warned about just before receiving adenosine?
src.key: The heart may stop for a few seconds
src.explanation: Adenosine may stop the heart for 2 to 3 seconds, and flushing, shortness of breath and chest burning can follow.

items.section_title: 2.7 · Objectives 1–8 — Class III: amiodarone, dofetilide, sotalol
items.html: Amiodarone counseling: the sun. Amiodarone causes photosensitivity and a blue-gray skin color, so sun protection is the counseling point.

src.question: A 58-year-old woman is starting long-term amiodarone. Which counseling point addresses a listed skin toxicity?
src.explanation: Amiodarone causes photosensitivity and a blue-gray skin color, so sun protection is the counseling point.

items.section_title: 2.7 · Objectives 1–8 — Class III: amiodarone, dofetilide, sotalol
items.html: Amiodarone raises other drugs. Amiodarone increases digoxin and warfarin, as well as flecainide, phenytoin and procainamide.

src.question: A 70-year-old man takes digoxin and warfarin. He is started on amiodarone for recurrent ventricular tachycardia. What happens to his digoxin and warfarin levels?
src.explanation: Amiodarone increases digoxin and warfarin, as well as flecainide, phenytoin and procainamide.

items.section_title: 2.7 · Objectives 1–8 — Class III: amiodarone, dofetilide, sotalol
items.html: Amiodarone and the thyroid, both ways. Amiodarone is an analog of thyroid hormone, and its thyroid abnormalities run in both directions; fatigue, weight gain and cold intolerance fit hypothyroidism.

src.question: A 62-year-old woman on amiodarone for a year reports fatigue, weight gain and feeling cold all the time. Which listed toxicity best fits?
src.explanation: Amiodarone is an analog of thyroid hormone, and its thyroid abnormalities run in both directions; fatigue, weight gain and cold intolerance fit hypothyroidism.

items.section_title: 2.5 · Objectives 1–7 — Class IC: flecainide, propafenone
items.html: Propafenone and the blood count. Propafenone's toxicity list includes agranulocytosis, anemia and thrombocytopenia.

src.question: Which drug lists agranulocytosis among its toxicities?
src.explanation: Propafenone's toxicity list includes agranulocytosis, anemia and thrombocytopenia.

items.section_title: 2.5 · Objectives 1–7 — Class IC: flecainide, propafenone
items.html: Flecainide and asthma. Bronchospasm is on flecainide's toxicity list (and propafenone's), a concern in asthma.

src.question: Which respiratory effect of flecainide matters in a patient with asthma?
src.explanation: Bronchospasm is on flecainide's toxicity list (and propafenone's), a concern in asthma.

items.section_title: 2.5 · Objectives 1–7 — Class IC: flecainide, propafenone
items.html: Which drugs are class IC. Flecainide is class IC (propafenone is the other); it blocks sodium and potassium channels in the ventricles.

src.question: Which drug is a class IC antiarrhythmic?
src.explanation: Flecainide is class IC (propafenone is the other); it blocks sodium and potassium channels in the ventricles.

items.section_title: 2.4 · Objectives 1–7 — Class IB: lidocaine
items.html: The class IB drug. Lidocaine is the class IB sodium channel blocker; it works mainly on sodium channels in ischemic tissue.

src.question: Which drug is the class IB antiarrhythmic?
src.explanation: Lidocaine is the class IB sodium channel blocker; it works mainly on sodium channels in ischemic tissue.

items.section_title: 2.8 · Objectives 1–7 — Class IV: verapamil, diltiazem
items.html: What verapamil and diltiazem treat. Verapamil and diltiazem are listed for supraventricular tachycardia (paroxysmal) and atrial fibrillation.

src.question: Which arrhythmia is a listed indication for verapamil and diltiazem?
src.explanation: Verapamil and diltiazem are listed for supraventricular tachycardia (paroxysmal) and atrial fibrillation.

items.section_title: 2.6 · Objectives 1–8 — Class II: beta blockers
items.html: Metoprolol and acebutolol: central effects. Central nervous system sedation and fatigue are listed for metoprolol and acebutolol, with congestive heart failure.

src.question: Which central nervous system effects are listed for metoprolol and acebutolol?
src.explanation: Central nervous system sedation and fatigue are listed for metoprolol and acebutolol, with congestive heart failure.

items.section_title: 2.6 · Objectives 1–8 — Class II: beta blockers
items.html: What propranolol treats. Propranolol is listed for supraventricular arrhythmias, ventricular ectopic beats and myocardial infarction.

src.question: Which arrhythmias are a listed indication for propranolol?
src.explanation: Propranolol is listed for supraventricular arrhythmias, ventricular ectopic beats and myocardial infarction.

items.section_title: 2.6 · Objectives 1–8 — Class II: beta blockers
items.html: Esmolol. Esmolol is the intravenous, short-acting beta blocker, listed beside the beta-1 selective agents metoprolol and acebutolol.

src.question: Which beta blocker is the intravenous, short-acting one?
src.explanation: Esmolol is the intravenous, short-acting beta blocker.

also.explanation: Esmolol is the intravenous, short-acting beta blocker.

also.question: Which beta blocker is given intravenously and is short acting?
also.explanation: Esmolol is the intravenous, short-acting beta blocker listed beside the beta-1 selective agents metoprolol and acebutolol.

items.section_title: 2.7 · Objectives 1–8 — Class III: amiodarone, dofetilide, sotalol
items.html: What sotalol treats. Sotalol is listed for atrial flutter and fibrillation and for ventricular tachyarrhythmia.

src.question: Which is a listed indication for sotalol?
src.explanation: Sotalol is listed for atrial flutter and fibrillation and for ventricular tachyarrhythmia.

items.section_title: 2.7 · Objectives 1–8 — Class III: amiodarone, dofetilide, sotalol
items.html: Amiodarone's ventricular indication. Amiodarone is listed for recurrent ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation resistant to other drugs.

src.question: Which ventricular arrhythmia is a listed indication for amiodarone?
src.explanation: Amiodarone is listed for recurrent ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation resistant to other drugs.

items.section_title: 2.7 · Objectives 1–8 — Class III: amiodarone, dofetilide, sotalol
items.html: Sotalol spans two classes. Sotalol has beta-blocking (class II) activity and inhibits potassium channels (class III).

src.question: Sotalol combines the actions of which two antiarrhythmic classes?
src.explanation: Sotalol has beta-blocking (class II) activity and inhibits potassium channels (class III).

items.section_title: 2.1 · Objectives 1–3 — Principles, the four classes and the indication trend
items.html: The others group. The classification lists adenosine and digitalis (digoxin) as the others, outside classes I to IV.

src.question: Outside classes I to IV, which two drugs make up the antiarrhythmic "others" group?
src.explanation: The classification lists adenosine and digitalis (digoxin) as the others, outside classes I to IV.

items.section_title: 2.9 · Objectives 1–8 — Miscellaneous agents: adenosine, digoxin, magnesium sulfate
items.html: Magnesium sulfate: the serious toxicity. Magnesium sulfate's listed toxicities are bradycardia, flushing, headache and respiratory paralysis, the most serious of these.

src.question: A 63-year-old man is receiving intravenous magnesium sulfate for torsades de pointes. Which listed toxicity is the most serious to watch for?
src.explanation: Magnesium sulfate's listed toxicities are bradycardia, flushing, headache and respiratory paralysis, the most serious of these.

items.section_title: 2.7 · Objectives 1–8 — Class III: amiodarone, dofetilide, sotalol
items.html: Intravenous amiodarone. Intravenous amiodarone terminates acute ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation; it is also listed for recurrent ventricular arrhythmias resistant to other drugs.

src.question: Which drug, given intravenously, terminates acute ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation?
src.explanation: Intravenous amiodarone terminates acute ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation; it is also listed for recurrent ventricular arrhythmias resistant to other drugs.

items.section_title: 2.9 · Objectives 1–8 — Miscellaneous agents: adenosine, digoxin, magnesium sulfate
items.html: Digoxin toxicity after amiodarone is added. Amiodarone increases digoxin, and digoxin toxicity lists nausea, vomiting, diarrhea and anorexia with confusion, delirium, headache, seizures and visual disturbances.

src.question: A 78-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation takes digoxin, and amiodarone was added two weeks ago. She now has anorexia, nausea, confusion and visual disturbances. Which is the most likely cause?
src.explanation: Amiodarone increases digoxin, and digoxin toxicity lists nausea, vomiting, diarrhea and anorexia with confusion, delirium, headache, seizures and visual disturbances.

items.section_title: 3.9 · Objectives 1–9 — Bronchodilators: beta-2 agonists, theophylline, anticholinergics
items.html: Theophylline and the stomach. Theophylline stimulates gastric acid, and nausea and heartburn are on the methylxanthine adverse effect list.

src.question: Which effect on the stomach is listed among theophylline's adverse effects?
src.explanation: Theophylline stimulates gastric acid, and nausea and heartburn are on the methylxanthine adverse effect list.

items.section_title: 3.10 · Objectives 1–10 — Controllers: corticosteroids, montelukast, mast cell stabilizers, biologics
items.html: Oral systemic corticosteroids in asthma. Oral systemic corticosteroids are the most potent option for suppressing airway inflammation, but their side effects limit their use, so they are used in asthma exacerbations.

src.question: Why are oral systemic corticosteroids reserved mainly for asthma exacerbations?
src.key: Their side effects limit their use
src.explanation: Oral systemic corticosteroids are the most potent option for suppressing airway inflammation, but their side effects limit their use, so they are used in asthma exacerbations.

items.section_title: 3.10 · Objectives 1–10 — Controllers: corticosteroids, montelukast, mast cell stabilizers, biologics
items.html: When to take cromolyn. Mast cell stabilizers such as cromolyn must be taken before the antigen insult; they remove the trigger rather than reverse bronchospasm.

src.question: When must cromolyn be taken to prevent an asthma attack?
src.explanation: Mast cell stabilizers such as cromolyn must be taken before the antigen insult; they remove the trigger rather than reverse bronchospasm.

items.section_title: 3.11 · Objectives 9–10 — Stepwise therapy, inhaler devices, technique and status asthmaticus
items.html: Spacers and valve holding chambers. Spacers and valve holding chambers are intended to retain the large particles emitted from the inhaler, leaving a higher proportion of smaller, respirable particles.

src.question: What does a spacer or valve holding chamber do to the particles the patient inhales?
src.key: Raises the share of small, respirable particles
src.explanation: Spacers and valve holding chambers are intended to retain the large particles emitted from the inhaler, leaving a higher proportion of smaller, respirable particles.

items.section_title: 3.12 · Objectives 1–10 — Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, smoking cessation and immunizations
items.html: Annual influenza vaccination in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease are at risk for significant morbidity and mortality from pneumonia caused by influenza, so annual vaccination is highly recommended.

src.question: Why is annual influenza vaccination highly recommended for patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease?
src.key: They risk serious pneumonia from influenza
src.explanation: Patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease are at risk for significant morbidity and mortality from pneumonia caused by influenza, so annual vaccination is highly recommended.

items.section_title: 3.12 · Objectives 1–10 — Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, smoking cessation and immunizations
items.html: High-risk chronic obstructive pulmonary disease groups. High risk (groups C and D) is two or more exacerbations per year with one or more leading to hospitalization; 0 or 1 exacerbation without hospitalization is low risk.

src.question: Which finding places a patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in a high-risk treatment group?
src.key: Two exacerbations a year, one hospitalized
src.explanation: High risk (groups C and D) is two or more exacerbations per year with one or more leading to hospitalization; 0 or 1 exacerbation without hospitalization is low risk.

items.section_title: 3.12 · Objectives 1–10 — Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, smoking cessation and immunizations
items.html: Long-term oxygen therapy. Long-term oxygen therapy is listed, for patients in any group, if there is chronic (persistent) hypoxemia.

src.question: For which patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is long-term oxygen therapy listed?
src.explanation: Long-term oxygen therapy is listed, for patients in any group, if there is chronic (persistent) hypoxemia.

items.section_title: 3.12 · Objectives 1–10 — Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, smoking cessation and immunizations
items.html: Nicotine replacement dose and duration. The dose and duration of nicotine replacement depend on the patient's level of dependence and point in therapy; the duration is between 6 and 12 weeks.

src.question: What determines the dose and duration of nicotine replacement therapy?
src.key: Dependence level and stage of treatment
src.explanation: The dose and duration of nicotine replacement depend on the patient's level of dependence and point in therapy; the duration is between 6 and 12 weeks.

items.section_title: 3.12 · Objectives 1–10 — Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, smoking cessation and immunizations
items.html: Nicotine replacement caution. Nicotine replacement calls for caution in patients with cardiovascular problems because of the chance of tachyarrhythmias and hypertension.

src.question: Nicotine replacement calls for caution in which patients?
src.explanation: Nicotine replacement calls for caution in patients with cardiovascular problems because of the chance of tachyarrhythmias and hypertension.

items.section_title: 3.11 · Objectives 9–10 — Stepwise therapy, inhaler devices, technique and status asthmaticus
items.html: Nebulizer: bigger dose, more side effects. A nebulizer allows passive inhalation, which suits children and older adults who cannot use a metered dose inhaler, but it delivers a bigger dose overall and may lead to more side effects; it must also be cleaned regularly.

src.question: A 4-year-old girl with asthma will use a nebulizer at home because she cannot use a metered dose inhaler. What should her parents be told about the nebulizer?
src.key: It gives a bigger dose, so more side effects
src.explanation: A nebulizer allows passive inhalation, which suits children and older adults who cannot use a metered dose inhaler, but it delivers a bigger dose overall and may lead to more side effects; it must also be cleaned regularly.

items.section_title: 3.4 · Objectives 1–9 — The hospital pneumonia antibiotics
items.html: Aminoglycoside toxicities. Aminoglycosides (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin) cause ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity; dose and frequency are adjusted on drug levels and depend heavily on renal function.

src.question: A 70-year-old man with ventilator-associated pneumonia receives tobramycin as part of broad-spectrum coverage. Which pair of toxicities should his monitoring target?
src.explanation: Aminoglycosides (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin) cause ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity; dose and frequency are adjusted on drug levels and depend heavily on renal function.

items.section_title: 3.2 · Objectives 1–3 and 9 — Community-acquired pneumonia
items.html: Hospitalized community-acquired pneumonia: cultures first. For hospitalized patients, blood and sputum cultures are obtained before antibiotics are given; outpatients, by contrast, do well with empiric antibiotics and are not routinely tested.

src.question: A 66-year-old woman is admitted to a hospital ward with community-acquired pneumonia. Before her first antibiotic dose, which step is recommended?
src.explanation: For hospitalized patients, blood and sputum cultures are obtained before antibiotics are given; outpatients, by contrast, do well with empiric antibiotics and are not routinely tested.

items.section_title: 3.9 · Objectives 1–9 — Bronchodilators: beta-2 agonists, theophylline, anticholinergics
items.html: Salmeterol is never used alone for asthma. Long-acting beta-2 agonists (formoterol, salmeterol) are not to be used alone for asthma; they are combined with an inhaled corticosteroid, as in salmeterol/fluticasone (Advair).

src.question: A 28-year-old man with persistent asthma asks to use salmeterol by itself as his one controller medicine. What should he be told?
src.key: It must be paired with an inhaled steroid
src.explanation: Long-acting beta-2 agonists (formoterol, salmeterol) are not to be used alone for asthma; they are combined with an inhaled corticosteroid, as in salmeterol/fluticasone (Advair).

items.section_title: 3.10 · Objectives 1–10 — Controllers: corticosteroids, montelukast, mast cell stabilizers, biologics
items.html: How to take cromolyn. Mast cell stabilizers (cromolyn, nedocromil) must be taken before the antigen insult and taken regularly; they may take up to 4 weeks to work.

src.question: A 25-year-old woman with allergic asthma is prescribed inhaled cromolyn sodium ahead of a long stay in a home with cats. How should she take it?
src.explanation: Mast cell stabilizers (cromolyn, nedocromil) must be taken before the antigen insult and taken regularly; they may take up to 4 weeks to work.

items.section_title: 3.2 · Objectives 1–3 and 9 — Community-acquired pneumonia
items.html: Intensive care unit pneumonia treatment. Intensive care unit treatment uses the same regimens, but all treatment begins intravenously, and coverage for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus is considered if warranted.

src.question: How does treatment of community-acquired pneumonia in the intensive care unit differ from treatment on the ward?
src.explanation: Intensive care unit treatment uses the same regimens, but all treatment begins intravenously, and coverage for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus is considered if warranted.

items.section_title: 3.2 · Objectives 1–3 and 9 — Community-acquired pneumonia
items.html: Timing of blood and sputum cultures. Blood and sputum cultures are obtained for hospitalized patients, and they are drawn prior to antibiotics.

src.question: For a patient hospitalized with community-acquired pneumonia, when should blood and sputum cultures be obtained?
src.explanation: Blood and sputum cultures are obtained for hospitalized patients, and they are drawn prior to antibiotics.

items.section_title: 3.2 · Objectives 1–3 and 9 — Community-acquired pneumonia
items.html: Outpatient community-acquired pneumonia. Outpatients do well with empiric antibiotics, and diagnostic tests are not routinely performed.

src.question: How is community-acquired pneumonia usually managed in the outpatient setting?
src.explanation: Outpatients do well with empiric antibiotics, and diagnostic tests are not routinely performed.

items.section_title: 3.1 · Objectives 1–3 — Acute bronchitis
items.html: Antihistamines in acute bronchitis. Antihistamines and sympathomimetics may be avoided because they dehydrate bronchial secretions and may prolong symptoms.

src.question: Why may antihistamines be avoided in acute bronchitis?
src.explanation: Antihistamines and sympathomimetics may be avoided because they dehydrate bronchial secretions and may prolong symptoms.

items.section_title: 3.3 · Objectives 3 and 9 — Nosocomial pneumonia: who gets it, what causes it, how wide to cover
items.html: Antipseudomonal fluoroquinolones and the atypicals. Ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin have good activity against the atypicals (Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Legionella) and good lung tissue penetration.

src.question: Besides Pseudomonas, the antipseudomonal fluoroquinolones have good activity against which group of pathogens?
src.explanation: Ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin have good activity against the atypicals (Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Legionella) and good lung tissue penetration.

items.section_title: 3.3 · Objectives 3 and 9 — Nosocomial pneumonia: who gets it, what causes it, how wide to cover
items.html: Health-care associated pneumonia criteria. Health-care associated pneumonia criteria include hemodialysis, nursing home residence, recent intravenous antibiotics, chemotherapy, wound care in the previous 30 days and a recent hospital stay.

src.question: Which history meets a listed criterion for health-care associated pneumonia?
src.explanation: Health-care associated pneumonia criteria include hemodialysis, nursing home residence, recent intravenous antibiotics, chemotherapy, wound care in the previous 30 days and a recent hospital stay.

items.section_title: 3.3 · Objectives 3 and 9 — Nosocomial pneumonia: who gets it, what causes it, how wide to cover
items.html: Switching to oral antibiotics. Antibiotics are switched to oral when or if possible because oral therapy is cheaper, as coverage is scaled back to the culture results.

src.question: Why is a patient switched to oral antibiotics when possible during pneumonia treatment?
src.explanation: Antibiotics are switched to oral when or if possible because oral therapy is cheaper, as coverage is scaled back to the culture results.

items.section_title: 3.4 · Objectives 1–9 — The hospital pneumonia antibiotics
items.html: Aminoglycoside dosing by levels. Aminoglycoside dose and frequency are adjusted based on levels, and they are highly dependent on renal function.

src.question: On what are aminoglycoside dose and frequency adjusted?
src.explanation: Aminoglycoside dose and frequency are adjusted based on levels, and they are highly dependent on renal function.

items.section_title: 3.4 · Objectives 1–9 — The hospital pneumonia antibiotics
items.html: Imipenem-cilastatin and seizures. Imipenem-cilastatin (Primaxin) is used with caution in patients with a seizure history; meropenem carries less seizure risk.

src.question: Which antipseudomonal agent is used with caution in a patient with a seizure history?
src.explanation: Imipenem-cilastatin (Primaxin) is used with caution in patients with a seizure history; meropenem carries less seizure risk.

items.section_title: 3.3 · Objectives 3 and 9 — Nosocomial pneumonia: who gets it, what causes it, how wide to cover
items.html: Two beta-lactams make an inappropriate regimen. Cefepime and piperacillin-tazobactam are both antipseudomonal beta-lactams; the partner must be an antipseudomonal fluoroquinolone or an aminoglycoside.

src.question: A proposed empiric regimen for nosocomial pneumonia with multidrug-resistant risk factors is cefepime, piperacillin-tazobactam and vancomycin. What makes it inappropriate?
src.explanation: Cefepime and piperacillin-tazobactam are both antipseudomonal beta-lactams; the partner must be an antipseudomonal fluoroquinolone or an aminoglycoside.

items.section_title: 3.4 · Objectives 1–9 — The hospital pneumonia antibiotics
items.html: Linezolid's drawback. Linezolid is expensive, though it has great methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus coverage, oral and intravenous forms, good lung penetration and no renal adjustment.

src.question: Which drawback is listed for linezolid?
src.explanation: Linezolid is expensive, though it has great methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus coverage, oral and intravenous forms, good lung penetration and no renal adjustment.

items.section_title: 3.4 · Objectives 1–9 — The hospital pneumonia antibiotics
items.html: Ceftazidime is rarely used. Ceftazidime (Fortaz) is not recommended because of rapid development of resistance and is rarely used; cefepime is the choice.

src.question: Why is ceftazidime rarely used as the antipseudomonal cephalosporin for nosocomial pneumonia?
src.explanation: Ceftazidime (Fortaz) is not recommended because of rapid development of resistance and is rarely used; cefepime is the choice.

items.section_title: 3.3 · Objectives 3 and 9 — Nosocomial pneumonia: who gets it, what causes it, how wide to cover
items.html: Famotidine as a nosocomial pneumonia risk factor. Histamine H2 blocker or antacid therapy is a modifiable risk factor for nosocomial pneumonia, and famotidine is a histamine H2 blocker.

src.question: Which drug's use is a modifiable risk factor for nosocomial pneumonia?
src.explanation: Histamine H2 blocker or antacid therapy is a modifiable risk factor for nosocomial pneumonia, and famotidine is a histamine H2 blocker.

items.section_title: 3.4 · Objectives 1–9 — The hospital pneumonia antibiotics
items.html: Piperacillin-tazobactam. Piperacillin-tazobactam (Zosyn) is the antipseudomonal penicillin with a beta-lactamase inhibitor, and it requires renal adjustment.

src.question: Which antipseudomonal agent is a penicillin combined with a beta-lactamase inhibitor?
src.explanation: Piperacillin-tazobactam (Zosyn) is the antipseudomonal penicillin with a beta-lactamase inhibitor, and it requires renal adjustment.

items.section_title: 3.3 · Objectives 3 and 9 — Nosocomial pneumonia: who gets it, what causes it, how wide to cover
items.html: Streamlining nosocomial pneumonia therapy. Therapy is streamlined once cultures and sensitivities are available, scaling back antibiotic coverage as the cultures return.

src.question: What should happen to empiric nosocomial pneumonia therapy once cultures and sensitivities return?
src.key: Narrow it to the culture results
src.explanation: Therapy is streamlined once cultures and sensitivities are available, scaling back antibiotic coverage as the cultures return.

items.section_title: 3.6 · Objectives 1–10 — Isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide
items.html: Rifampin is rarely used alone. Rifampin is rarely used alone because rapid tolerance develops; in tuberculosis it is always combined.

src.question: Why is rifampin rarely used alone?
src.explanation: Rifampin is rarely used alone because rapid tolerance develops; in tuberculosis it is always combined.

items.section_title: 3.6 · Objectives 1–10 — Isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide
items.html: Isoniazid resistance. Resistance comes from mutation in the DNA coding for the activating enzyme, the bacterial catalase-peroxidase.

src.question: How does Mycobacterium tuberculosis become resistant to isoniazid?
src.key: Mutation in the gene for its activating enzyme
src.explanation: Resistance comes from mutation in the DNA coding for the activating enzyme, the bacterial catalase-peroxidase, so isoniazid is never activated.

items.section_title: 3.6 · Objectives 1–10 — Isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide
items.html: Rifampin's interactions. Rifampin induces cytochrome P450 enzymes (CYP1A2, CYP2C9 and CYP3A4), which is how it interacts with anticoagulants, contraceptives, digoxin, ketoconazole and theophylline.

src.question: Rifampin interacts with anticoagulants, contraceptives, digoxin and theophylline through which action?
src.explanation: Rifampin induces cytochrome P450 enzymes (CYP1A2, CYP2C9 and CYP3A4), which is how it interacts with anticoagulants, contraceptives, digoxin, ketoconazole and theophylline.

items.section_title: 3.6 · Objectives 1–10 — Isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide
items.html: Ethambutol helps the other agents. Ethambutol inhibits mycolic acid incorporation into membranes, and the weakened cell wall allows other agents better access.

src.question: What does ethambutol's weakening of the mycobacterial cell wall do for combination therapy?
src.key: It lets other agents in more easily
src.explanation: Ethambutol inhibits mycolic acid incorporation into membranes, and the weakened cell wall allows other agents better access.

items.section_title: 3.5 · Objectives 1, 3 and 9 — Tuberculosis: the organism and combination therapy
items.html: Why cell-division drugs work less well against tuberculosis. Mycobacterium tuberculosis is very slow growing and can exist in dormant states for long periods, so drugs that act on dividing cells work less well.

src.question: Why do antimicrobials that act on cell division work less well against Mycobacterium tuberculosis?
src.key: It grows slowly and can lie dormant
src.explanation: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is very slow growing and can exist in dormant states for long periods, so drugs that act on dividing cells work less well.

items.section_title: 3.6 · Objectives 1–10 — Isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide
items.html: What pyrazinamide adds. Pyrazinamide decreases the duration of combined therapy; it is given during the first two months only.

src.question: What does pyrazinamide add to combined tuberculosis therapy?
src.explanation: Pyrazinamide decreases the duration of combined therapy; it is given during the first two months only.
